# Mode transitions in a viscoplastic rheology

Rohan Byrne

## Abstract

The question of the origins of plate tectonics is fundamentally a question of tectonic mode transitions. One possible factor that could catalyse the breakup of the early Earth’s stagnant lid is stress localisation at the margins of buoyant crust [(Rey, Coltice, and Flament 2014\)](https://paperpile.com/c/a2pYSk/Gndc). A program to investigate this hypothesis is here presented as fit for completion at a PhD level. Progress toward the objective has included the development of new tools for suite modelling and a thorough replication study of [(Louis Moresi and Solomatov 1998\)](https://paperpile.com/c/a2pYSk/pBL7).

## 1 \- Introduction

This progress report is presented in fulfilment of the requirements of the extended confirmation process.

The purpose of this research is to ascertain what underlying parameters most strongly control a planet’s choice of tectonic mode by conducting in-depth modelling of mode transitions within a comparative planetology framework. In particular, this project will investigate the controls that surface chemistries and geometries can place on the interior. Modelling results will be properly constrained by reference to local Earth-like planets, particularly Mars, Venus, and the early Earth.

Progress toward this objective thus far, in outline, has comprised:

- The development of a code library implementing a new interface for the Underworld2 package designed to streamline suite modelling.

- Benchmarking of the code against the Blankenbach standards [(Blankenbach et al. 1989\)](https://paperpile.com/c/a2pYSk/p413).

- A replication study of [(Louis Moresi and Solomatov 1998\)](https://paperpile.com/c/a2pYSk/pBL7).

- Extension of the replicated study to very wide aspect ratios and periodic boundaries.

An additional objective building on the above is the modelling of the impact of lithospheric heterogeneities on the stability of the upper boundary layer, early steps toward which were the focus of the previous confirmation report. This work is underway at present but no additional results to that end are presented in this report.

This progress report will begin with an overview of the theoretical background and general methodology of the project. This will be followed by a brief account of each of the steps made thus far, with details and extra data contained in the appendices. The results will be discussed collectively before an outline of the planned research program is given, along with some concluding thoughts on progress made.

## 2 \- Background

The topic of this research program is the phenomenon of tectonic modes and mode transitions. A tectonic mode can be defined as an organised mantle flow regime which is either steady-state or periodic. Plate tectonics on Earth, episodic overturn on Venus [(Turcotte et al. 1999\)](https://paperpile.com/c/a2pYSk/aKLo), possible stagnant lid convection on Mars [(Weizman et al. 2001\)](https://paperpile.com/c/a2pYSk/P6xZ), and heat pipe volcanism on Io [(Moore, Simon, and Webb 2017\)](https://paperpile.com/c/a2pYSk/kjaL) are all examples of distinct tectonic modes. Tectonic modes are fundamentally a response to absolute and relative rates of radiogenic heating and secular cooling [(O’Neill et al. 2016/6)](https://paperpile.com/c/a2pYSk/BfnL): the ratio of these drivers is the so-called ‘Urey ratio’ [(Urey 1955\)](https://paperpile.com/c/a2pYSk/r3a1) whose value, based on geoneutrino measurements, is now evaluated at around one third for Earth [(Mareschal et al. 2012\)](https://paperpile.com/c/a2pYSk/zzqi). low Urey ratio projects unrealistic temperatures on the early Earth if present levels of surface cooling are held constant [(Korenaga 2003\)](https://paperpile.com/c/a2pYSk/sTxn), and because different tectonic modes can be shown to be more or less effective at disbursing Earth’s heat budget [(Höink, Lenardic, and Jellinek 2013/8)](https://paperpile.com/c/a2pYSk/dgxE), it is implicit that the Earth experienced alternative tectonic modes before transitioning into plate tectonics.

The question of Earth’s uniqueness therefore descends on two points:

1) What caused the Earth to transition into modern plate tectonics? Supporting questions involve the timing and mechanism of this transition and the nature of the preceding tectonic mode or modes.  
2) What has prevented the Earth from transitioning out of plate tectonics? The persistence of modern tectonics for billions of years argues for the existence of either a ‘switch’ \- a chance deflection of the Earth down a bifurcation in parameter space \- or a ‘ratchet’ \- an irreversible time-dependent force such as secular cooling, diminishing of radiogenic heat, increasing heat from the sun, the establishment of the biosphere, or the global chemical differentiation of the Earth.

Of course, it is not possible within a single PhD to follow all these lines of evidence. However, one promising avenue of inquiry, addressing both prongs of the conundrum, invokes the role of continents.

On the modern Earth, continental crust interacts with global geodynamics directly via thermal insulation and conditioning of flow geometries [(Lenardic et al. 2005; Grigné, Labrosse, and Tackley 2005; Zhong and Liu 2016/1)](https://paperpile.com/c/a2pYSk/llts+p2Q6+ShWP), as well as indirectly via climate feedbacks [(Weller, Lenardic, and O’Neill 2015\)](https://paperpile.com/c/a2pYSk/hAWc) and sequestration of heat-producing elements [(Huang et al. 2013\)](https://paperpile.com/c/a2pYSk/VZii). Much of the modern continental crust appears to have its genesis at 3 Ga [(Hawkesworth, Cawood, and Dhuime 2013; Næraa et al. 2012; Labrosse and Jaupart 2007\)](https://paperpile.com/c/a2pYSk/ZXMA+oS1i+B3mt), perhaps due to rapid thickening of pre-existing differentiated material caused by elevated surface stresses during the catastrophic failure of a global immobile lid [(Beall, Moresi, and Cooper 2018\)](https://paperpile.com/c/a2pYSk/eag7). Having been created in one or more such events, perhaps during an intermediary ‘episodic overturn’ regime between stagnant and mobile tectonic modes [(Louis Moresi and Solomatov 1998; Ernst 2009/6)](https://paperpile.com/c/a2pYSk/pBL7+L7IZ), the cratons may have subsequently shepherded the Earth toward modern plate tectonics through the supercontinent cycle [(Yoshida and Santosh 2011/3; Zhong et al. 2007\)](https://paperpile.com/c/a2pYSk/jAr3+RIZf). Continents would therefore be implicated as one possible ‘ratchet’-type control on Earth’s tectonic mode, stabilising the plate tectonic regime. The absence of a global material dichotomy on the other local Earth-like planets lends credence to this theory.

While the significance of continents to the history of plate tectonics is well-attested, the role of buoyant lithospheric material in the pre-tectonic era is less well understood. Zircon data suggests that continental crust was being formed, eroded, and recycled even in early Hadean times [(Watson and Harrison 2005\)](https://paperpile.com/c/a2pYSk/vfWD), while Earth’s many oceanic plateaux abundantly demonstrate that it is possible to create buoyant crustal features through vertical tectonics alone. Could lenses of buoyant crust in the sluggish early Earth have acted as stress foci, catalysing the transition to a more vigorous and organised mode? If so, the continents might be implicated in both triggering and sustaining modern plate tectonics on our planet. Testing this hypothesis has constituted the first major task of the PhD program.

## 3 \- Methods

This research program will explore the question of tectonic modes and mode transitions through numerical modelling of planetary interiors. Model results will be cross-referenced with real physical data and used to constrain the range of plausible hypotheses for the establishment of plate tectonics on Earth and its absence on the other local rocky planets. The primary goal is to build a model that self-consistently exhibits a transition from the primordial stagnant regime to modern plate tectonics, either directly via a single transition or indirectly via multiple transitions through intermediate tectonic modes. By driving the model to be as parsimonious as possible while still producing the target features, some insight may be gained into the fundamental planetary parameters enabling or prohibiting different tectonic modes. This is a necessary first step toward a predictive model of tectonics that would indicate how common or rare the Earth really is.

### 3.1 \- Numerical methods

This study uses the *Underworld2* code to solve the Stokes and advection-diffusion equations for large-scale mantle convection simulations.

*Underworld2* is a fast, robust, scalable particle-in-cell finite element numerical modelling code designed for large-scale geodynamics applications [(L. Moresi, Dufour, and Muhlhaus 2002; L. Moresi, Dufour, and \-B. Muuhlhaus 2003; L. Moresi et al. 2007; Dyksterhuis et al. 2007\)](https://paperpile.com/c/a2pYSk/kUZH+uFvu+CS0n+QEjb). Within the *Underworld* framework, the mantle and lithosphere are modelled as a complex convecting fluid in a state of creeping flow obeying the incompressibility and infinite Prandtl assumptions. These limitations permit a particular linearisation of the Navier-Stokes and advection-diffusion equations which can be looped over many times to achieve a robust approximation of nonlinear fluid dynamics.

The numerical formulation begins with the incompressible density function:

\=0T

where is the change in density as a function of the change in temperature T, a reference density  
 0, and a thermal expansivity coefficient .

The temperature field defines the density everywhere, density and gravity define pressure, and pressure defines velocity. These quantities are related by the linearised Stokes equations:

\-(D) \+ p \= gz

Dij=(ui/xj+uj/xi

*u \= 0* 

Here(D)is the gradient of the strain rate tensor Daccounting for a dynamic viscosity, pis the pressure gradient, gzdenotes the buoyancy force in response to a density anomaly, andu= 0 is the conservation equation asserting that the velocity field nowhere diverges. This linearised Stokes equations can be solved by a wide variety of standard methods in calculus. Non-linear behaviour is introduced at this point, though, as the temperature field must be updated by the velocity field to account for the advection and diffusion of heat:

∂T∂t=2T \-u⋅∇T

where Tin this represents temperature, 2is the Laplace operator, andis the thermal diffusivity.

The updated temperature field is used to redefine the density field and the whole loop repeats again, with no exact solution beyond trivial cases. *Underworld* uses powerful libraries built in *C* to increment this computationally taxing loop in parallel, converging on a sufficient approximation using the calculus of variations [(L. Moresi, Dufour, and \-B. Muuhlhaus 2003\)](https://paperpile.com/c/a2pYSk/uFvu).

Since the release of *Underworld2*, the tremendous mathematical complexity of this process is belied by a flexible, versatile, and accessible new interface, written in *Python*. Among the many advantages of the *Python* wrapper is the facility it provides for networking with other scientific computing codes: for example, statistical analysis packages like *MatPlotLib* and *Pandas*, the *Badlands* geomorphology code, and even Google’s powerful open-source *TensorFlow* software for massively parallel machine learning. The *Underworld2* platform powered all of the modelling used in this study.

### 3.2 \- Viscoplastic rheology

One of the key coefficients of the constitutive equations is the viscosity, or momentum diffusivity. While simple fluids like water can be modelled under a constant viscosity assumption, geodynamic modelling must account for strongly variable viscosity in the mantle [(Foster 1969\)](https://paperpile.com/c/a2pYSk/Yzvg). Moreover, mantle materials fail brittlely at the surface, which would seem to challenge the characterisation of the Earth as a convecting viscous fluid. This is particularly pertinent to plate tectonics and mode transitions, which are fundamentally a balance between brittle and ductile processes within the mantle.

[(Louis Moresi and Solomatov 1998\)](https://paperpile.com/c/a2pYSk/pBL7) have previously demonstrated a dynamic stagnant-to-mobile lid transition using a viscoplastic rheology based on the second strain-rate invariant. Their viscoplastic rheology uses a temperature-dependent (Arrhenius) ‘creep’ viscosity and a strain rate and depth-dependent (von Mises) yielding viscosity, with the latter coming into force whenever and wherever stress exceeds a specified yield stress value. The formulation is as follows:

**Temperature-dependent viscosity:**  
**(T) \= B exp QRT**  
where B is a constant, Q is an activation energy, and R is the gas constant. However, this law can be decomposed according to the Frank-Kamenetski approximation [(White and Johns 1987\)](https://paperpile.com/c/a2pYSk/qjzM):  
\= exp \- T  
where \=Q TTi2and Tiis the interior temperature of the convection cell. In a dimensionless formulation, can be further reduced to a function of the proportional viscosity change associated with the temperature change across the upper boundary layer:  
\= exp   
This relation yields the final temperature-dependent viscosity function:  
T \= exp (-1 \* log T)  
which simplified becomes:  
T \= 1T  
I.e. the temperature-dependent viscosity is proportional to the inverse of the viscosity contrast to the power of T.

**Strain rate-dependent viscosity:**  
**yield(D) \=yield2D**  
where D is the second strain-rate invariant and yieldis the yield stress:  
yield \= c0 \+ gz  
where c0is the yield stress at zero hydrostatic pressure and is the coefficient of friction. The yield stress can be non-dimensionalised to the form:  
'yield \= 0  \+ 1 z'  
where 0is the cohesive yield stress and 1 is the depth-dependent yield stress.

Apart from the parameters governing the rheology (the viscosity contrast and the reference yield stresses), the one other independent variable in Moresi and Solomatov’s formulation is the Rayleigh number, a measure of the instability of a fluid due to temperature contrasts:

Ra \= gTd3

where gis gravitational acceleration, is the density, is the thermal expansivity, Tis a reference temperature contrast across the domain, dis a characteristic length scale, is thermal diffusivity, and is the dynamic viscosity.

With dimensionless parameters, every factor of Ra devolves to unit except , the variable density. For this study, then, Rayleigh number is effectively equivalent to the coefficient of the temperature-dependent density function. Higher Rayleigh numbers will therefore reflect a stronger buoyancy force and will tend to support more vigorous convection.

Using this very parsimonious viscoplastic rheology, [(Louis Moresi and Solomatov 1998\)](https://paperpile.com/c/a2pYSk/pBL7) were able to model both stagnant and mobile regimes, as well as a third, intermediate tectonic mode oscillating between the two, which they dubbed the ‘episodic overturn’ mode. This study reproduces these results and extends them by recreating the same strain-rate dependent viscosity in the *Underworld2* geodynamic numerical modelling code, a modern successor to the *CITCOM* code used by the original authors [(L.-N. Moresi and Solomatov 1995\)](https://paperpile.com/c/a2pYSk/Auqp). 

### 3.3 \- Modelling approach & tools

To simplify the process of producing, analysing, and storing the suites of model-runs the project parameters demanded, a *Python* module is being developed implementing a new interface for defining and manipulating *Underworld* models. The new module separates the essential physics of a model from any physically meaningless aspects of the code, and provides a single interface for all variable input parameters so that a model can be run with a single function call. This opens the possibility of meta-scripts that generate, run, analyse, aggregate, and properly store large suites of models all without user intervention, significantly streamlining the exploration of parameter space.

In essence, *PlanetEngine* treats each ‘model’ as a composite of three different objects:

1) The ‘model’ proper, which hosts all attributes of a model system that a) impact the physical outputs of the model, and b) *cannot* be smoothly varied. These include all of its physical laws and associated numerical methods, boundary conditions, dimensions, and state variables, as well as certain integer parameters such as the resolution and particle density.  
2) A ‘parameter’ object comprising all smoothly variable, physically relevant attributes of the system. Collectively the parameters define an n-dimensional real number array homologous with an n-dimensional physical space, the parameter space, in which a particular set of parameters can be treated as a coordinate and a set of sets of parameters represents a volume.  
3) An ‘options’ object that prescribes all behaviours of the model that do not impact its physical behaviours. These include properties like the data sampling rate, the designated end condition, preferences for saving, storing, and restarting a model run, and any necessary metadata such as the project name. The options object also specifies a model’s initial conditions, on the grounds that all instances of a given model run with given parameters share a single output space and will converge on the same behaviours if they approach the same state.

Conceptually, *PlanetEngine* treats modelling analogously to real-life field work. A model is fed a coordinate in parameter space \- the ‘parameters’ object \- to define a model ‘case’. Within each case, the variables of state define a coordinate in output space, and a chain of states defines a curve. A particular model run can then be thought of as a ‘traverse’ of output space, starting from a specific and arbitrary ‘locality’ (the initial state), and journeying freely along a path determined by the model physics up to an equally arbitrary endpoint. Along the way, some localities are captured in perfect detail, defining a new ‘state’, while the majority of others are observed more superficially. The start point, end point, and sampling behaviour are all assigned to the model by the ‘options’ object.

With enough traverses over a particular model case, it becomes possible to define a flow field over the output space, predicting how any given model run will evolve given a particular initial condition. Although this ‘topography’ is impossible to fully visualise for non-trivial models, its extremely high dimensionality will be amenable to machine learning processes, which can efficiently search for symmetries (for example, loops of behaviour) to reveal the hidden parameters of the model. Once a particular model case is effectively characterised, the newly-derived output parameters can be assigned over input parameter space and subjected to the same analysis, revealing the fundamental latent variables implicit within the model system as a whole.

*PlanetEngine* is an interface for *Underworld2* tailor-made to implement this workflow. The module has enjoyed two months of active development and now exists as a completely functional, but not yet fully-featured, working prototype. An early iteration of the code, available on the author’s public *Github* page ([https://github.com/rsbyrne](https://github.com/rsbyrne)), generated all the data for this report. Completion of the module is targeted for the end of 2018\.

## 4 \- Results

### 4.1 \- Isoviscous convection benchmarks

The code was first tested against the benchmarks published in [(Blankenbach et al. 1989\)](https://paperpile.com/c/a2pYSk/p413). The model parameters were as follows.

- Square domain with four frictionless sides and Dirichlet top and bottom temperature conditions

- Initial degree 1 sinusoidal perturbation of the temperature field

- Isoviscous regime with parsimonious buoyancy function (= Ra \* temperature field)

- A square mesh was used (no mesh refinement)

The controlled variables were the Rayleigh number (1e4 \- 1e9) and the resolution (32 \- 256). The outputs of interest were the velocity root mean square and the Nusselt number. The Nusselt number is defined as the ratio of convective to conductive heat transfer across the domain; in a dimensionless framework (i.e. a domain of unit height, temperature contrast, and diffusivity), it is equivalent to the surface temperature gradient. Higher Nusselt numbers imply more vigorous convection and a thinner upper boundary layer.

The first round of benchmarks were run for Rayleigh numbers 1e4, 1e5, and 1e6, and resolutions of 32 and 64 cells. The models were run to a steady state defined by the time derivative of the Nusselt number remaining below 1 for a dimensionless model time of at least 0.01 units. Later, a second round of benchmarks were run which go beyond the Blankenbach reported values, pushing up to resolutions of 128 and 256 and Rayleigh numbers of 1e7 and 1e8.

*Fig 1: Table of Nu and VRMS compared to reported values (percentage deviation from benchmark values in brackets).*

The resulting VRMS and Nusselt values were in close agreement to benchmark values (\< 1% error) once an appropriate resolution was reached. Nusselt number proved more sensitive to under-resolution than VRMS due to the failure of coarse grids to represent the fine boundary layer. For this reason high Rayleigh numbers demand ever higher resolutions to appropriately model: Ra of greater than 1e6 should not be modelled at less than 128 resolution.

There are several key observations to be made. Firstly, it is clear that Rayleigh numbers greater than 1e6 cannot be explored faithfully at resolutions less than 128 cells without mesh refinement due to under-resolution of the boundary layer. Secondly, plots of Nusselt number over model time reveal that for high Rayleigh numbers (greater than 1e5) the choice of initial conditions substantially influences the time required to achieve a steady state. This is because metastable convective aspect ratios preferred by certain initial conditions can persist for a prolonged timespan before the correct convection geometry is achieved. This problem is exacerbated by under-resolution to the extent that low-resolution high-Ra models can become stuck in the metastable regime effectively indefinitely, returning a false positive for the steady-state criterion and ending prematurely. Mobile boundary layer instabilities are another problem which can take many overturn cycles to resolve. However, given sufficient time and resolution, all systems modelled settled ultimately into a single square convection cell with a boundary layer thickness inversely related to the Rayleigh number.

*Fig. 4: Inset of the above. Later in the model, the anti-clockwise spiral ‘kinks’ and reverses chirality multiple times in ever faster succession. Each ‘kink’ represents a dateable event in the otherwise orderly journey towards a steady state.*

**Impact of initial conditions**

To ascertain the impact of initial conditions on the time to achieve a steady state, a sample benchmark model was rerun with the sinusoidal perturbation substituted for a pseudo-randomised linear temperature gradient. The model chosen for revisiting used a Rayleigh number of 1e6 and a resolution of 64 cells. When allowed to evolve naturally, without the imposed initial degree-1 geometry, the system first attains a metastable two-cell geometry, with one upwelling in the middle of the domain and downwellings along both walls. Although the plume is attracted to the frictionless sidewalls, because of the symmetric initial conditions it is for a time unable to discriminate between them. The oscillations of the indecisive plume are responsible for the jagged profile visible between model times 0.02 \- 0.03. Eventually, however, the plume approaches one of the sidewalls and displaces the downwelling plume there, causing the system to collapse into a single-cell regime. The more efficient square aspect ratio supports a steeper geotherm and consequent higher Nusselt number.

*![][image4]*  
*Fig. 5: Although the single upwelling zone is swiftly established, it is trapped in the middle of the domain until model time 0.04. The two-cell system eventually collapses at roughly the same time as in the prior, sinusoidal case.*

### 4.2 \- Viscoplastic benchmarking study

In [(Louis Moresi and Solomatov 1998\)](https://paperpile.com/c/a2pYSk/pBL7), the authors robustly demonstrated the facility of a bifurcating temperature- and strain rate-dependent rheology to achieve both mobile and stagnant regimes given appropriate yield stresses. More significantly, the authors described an intermediate ‘episodic overturn’ regime, in which a dominant stagnant lid was periodically broken and reprocessed. Since that time, episodic overturn has been recognised as a genuine tectonic mode, with Venus’ youthful surface often cited as a canonical example [(Turcotte et al. 1999\)](https://paperpile.com/c/a2pYSk/aKLo).

This replication study hewed as close as possible to the original paper. Where ambiguity has existed in aspects of the model setup, reasonable guesses have been made to complete the picture. For the main model series, the following parameters were used:

- Rayleigh number \= 1e7  
- Viscosity contrast \= 3e4 (with viscosity values clipped at a minimum value of 1\)  
- A square grid of 64 cells with 12 particles per cell. Although the original paper employed grid refinement, with the reported effect of increasing the vertical resolution at the top of the boundary by 50%, lack of detail on the exact refinement method used recommended in favour of eschewing this feature. (The possible effects of insufficient resolution on the results will be discussed hereafter).  
- An initial temperature field derived from the isoviscous case at steady state for the same Rayleigh number.  
- Depth-dependent yield stress 1= 1e7.  
- Variable cohesive yield stress 0from 1e5 to 1e6.

Models were run for a dimensionless time of 0.6, double to triple the runtime used in the original paper. Though the central results of [(Louis Moresi and Solomatov 1998\)](https://paperpile.com/c/a2pYSk/pBL7) were recreated with good correspondence, certain borderline cases varied significantly from the previously reported results.

All three modes, including the episodic mode, presented themselves at the target parameters. The latent phases of the episodic mode tracked the stagnant lid case, with Nusselt number peaks exceeding the mobile case and approaching the isoviscous endmember case for this Rayleigh number at Nu \= 31\. This affirms that the episodic regime has indeed been properly resolved, becoming maximally stagnant and maximally mobile with each cycle. The mobile case itself reaches a steady state at 10.31, comparable and likely related to the 10.257 Nu value associated with isoviscous convection for this resolution for a Rayleigh number of 1e5, two orders lower than the value of 1e7 imposed here, which suggests that 1e5 is an ‘effective’ Rayleigh number for this case.

Deviating from the original paper, the new results suggest the episodic case at this value of 0 is doubly periodic, with pairs of of failure events occurring in regular close succession, while intervals of variable duration separate each pair. While the small period appears to match the reported results almost exactly, the longer period is a novelty. Closer inspection of the velocity field preceding each failure event reveals that the pairs of failures, while superficially similar, arise from fundamentally different eddy configurations in the mantle; the first involves a simple transition from a two-cell to a single-celled convection system, while the second has a significantly more complex evolution involving many small cells and multi-layered convection. The regular timing between failure pairs suggests the second failure in each is necessarily and wholly consequent to the first.

The timing of subsequent failures is a function of the amount of time it takes for a single-cell convection geometry to re-establish itself after the disruption of the velocity field by the sudden and total collapse of the upper boundary layer.*

The occurrence of the paired regime is puzzling, but not alarming. Indeed, an almost perfect fit for the reported Nu profile at 4e5 can be found in the replication data at 3e5, merely 10% below the expected 0\. Generally, this replication study recognises a variety of different styles of episodicity not explicitly documented in the original paper, from a simple regular mode at various frequencies, to paired failures, irregular interval episodicity, very long wavelength features at the high yield stress end, and bizarre double wall failures at yield stresses below 1e5 as the viscosity function hits at arbitrarily limited floor at value 1\.

The various discrepancies between this replication study and the original paper [(Louis Moresi and Solomatov 1998\)](https://paperpile.com/c/a2pYSk/pBL7) demand explanation, and the first most obvious attribute to check is the resolution. Because the episodic case for 0=1.5e5is extremely close to the mobile transition, it is a good target for a resolution check. The case was rerun for resolutions of 128 and 32 cells.

![][image16]

*Fig. 9: A Nusselt plot of the tests, timeshifted around the fifth of nine peaks in all models. Low resolution models take longer to reach a steady state; once they do, however, resolution has almost no impact on the shape of the curve.*

The test confirms that neither the tectonic mode nor the fundamental parameters of the system have been significantly impacted by under-resolution. This is in agreement with the findings of the original authors, who acquired useful data even with a very coarse mesh of 32 cells.

### 4.3 \- Viscoplasticity in wide aspects

Out of concern for the impacts of an unrealistically restrictive horizontal length scale on the global flow pattern, [(Louis Moresi and Solomatov 1998\)](https://paperpile.com/c/a2pYSk/pBL7) concluded their study with a reproduction of the main findings in a wide aspect ratio (4:1). They observed no change to the tectonic mode exhibited at each value of 0(1e5, 4e5, and 1e6) but did note that the style of convection within each mode appeared to be more volatile and complex, particularly for the episodic case.

These results were reproduced at a lower resolution and for less model time than for the unit case due to resource restrictions. Nonetheless, all three models returned results largely analogous to those obtained for the unit aspect ratio, in agreement with the original authors. No anomalous behaviour was observed in the episodic case, although the periodicity of failure was more complex due to the formation of two semi-independent downwelling zones on each wall which tended to collapse alternately.

However, there were some notable anomalies. One such anomaly was a late mode transition in the purported stable stagnant-lid endmember, which occurred a substantial quiescence. This was the result of the migration of a downwelling to the left sidewall and the subsequent establishment of a single, wide-aspect convection cell, which drove a sustained collapse of the stagnant lid that showed no sign of abating when the imposed time limit was reached for this model. Although this behaviour was not observed in the original paper, it is not altogether surprising that the mantle flow should eventually achieve a wider geometry to match its environment. It does, however, suggest that the true stagnant endmember for the 4:1 aspect ratio may be found at an even higher yield stress. A thorough parameter search of this model for very long run times is called for.

![][image17]

*Fig. 10: The velocity field of the stagnant case (0= 1e6) which developed after a model time of 0.15. The establishment of single-cell convection allowed a sustained mobilisation of the upper boundary layer. The uniformity of the surface velocity is a hallmark of plate-like behaviour.*

The other interesting discrepancy between the wide aspect model and its unit equivalent is the apparent relocation of the episodic-to-stagnant (or indeed, pseudo-stagnant) mode transition, which in the unit model was constrained between 0=4e5 \- 5e5. The 5e5 case here is another episodic mode, slightly less vigorous but of equivalent style and identical frequency to the 4e4 case. The location of the transition to the higher stress mode is not known and also warrants further investigation.

![][image18]![][image19]

*Fig. 11: Nu and surface velocity RMS plots for a series between 0=1e5 \-1e6 for an aspect ratio of 4\. The upper limit of the episodic regime has moved up 20% from 0=4e5to the vicinity of 0=5e5*. *The mobile regime is relatively unchanged but the stagnant endmember at 1e6 has an anomalous late wall failure and subsequent transition to degree-one convection.*

![][image20]![][image21]![][image22]

*Fig. 12: Typical temperature fields of the mobile (top), episodic (middle), and stagnant (bottom) regimes. The wide aspect models broadly replicate their unit aspect equivalents, but with additional behaviours; the stagnant regime, for example, exhibits a very long-wavelength failure event after the timestep depicted, and appears to be destined for a single global convection cell under a stagnant lid, while the episodic regime alternately fails on one wall and then the other.*

### 4.4 \- Impact of periodic domains and material contrasts

While the original authors sought to constrain the impact of different aspect ratios, the effect of the frictionless boundary walls themselves was not ascertained. In this study, the core series from yield stress 1e5 to 1e6 was recreated with periodic (wrapping) boundaries. 

The effect was emphatic: complete lid stagnation for all values yield stress attempted. The cause is evident from the velocity field: unable to achieve a single square convection cell, the circulation has converged on a stable double cell geometry. The narrow aspect of each cell leads to weak currents in the upper mantle. Although the weaker cases do see some yielding in the upper boundary, the plastic envelope is never large enough, nor the underlying velocities large enough, to precipitate a failure.

![][image23]

*Fig. 13: Four cases from the benchmark suite reproduced in a periodic 1:1 domain. All cases immediately stagnated, with the only variation being the time taken to reach maximum lid thickness.*

*Fig. 14: Temperature and velocity fields for the 0=1e5case at steady state. It is almost identical to the other cases surveyed, the sole difference being very minor yielding in the upper boundary layer.*

Because the imposition of periodic boundaries effectively halves the permitted maximum aspect of each convection cell, the series was re-run with an box ratio of 2:1. The wide-aspect periodic model resulted in global circulation which was indistinguishable from two 1:1 freeslip models mirrored and connected at equivalent walls. The Nusselt and surface velocity plots reflect this, with the only deviation from the behaviour of the original suite being the greater time taken to reach steady state, the overall lesser Nusselt numbers as a consequence of the low resolution (32 cells), and a more regular frequency for the episodic regime (though the parameters of each failure event remained the same. All tectonic modes manifested themselves at exactly the yield stresses expected. The results very strongly argue that the free-slip condition imposed in the original study had no distortive effect whatsoever.

![][image24]

![][image25]

*Fig. 15: Viscoplastic rheology in a periodic domain of aspect 2\. The three canonical cases from the original paper are modelled, as is the borderline 5e5 case which was previously found to be close to the episodic/stagnant transition. Slightly lower Nusselt numbers compared to the original case may be attributed to the low resolution.![][image26]*![][image27]![][image28]![][image29]

*Fig. 16: Temperature fields for the periodic boundary model. Left-right and top-bottom: the mobile case at 0=1e5, the episodic case at 0=4e5, and the two, virtually identical stagnant lid cases at 0=5e5, 0 \=1e6*.

![][image30]![][image31]

*Fig. 17: Temperature fields of the episodic case at 4e5 during and immediately after a failure event. The cause of lid failure, and the control on its timing, is the transition from a convection geometry with two small, weak convection cells to one large, strong one. The larger cell supports a single strong central upwelling, pushing the convecting mantle into the brittle envelope and precipitating a failure. Overturn equilibrates the temperature field and some time must pass before the subsequent small cells merge and renew the degree-one geometry.*

## 5 \- Discussion

Although the findings of [(Louis Moresi and Solomatov 1998\)](https://paperpile.com/c/a2pYSk/pBL7) were substantively replicated in this study, with several discrepancies attributable to slight differences in the underlying numerical methods used and other minor differences in the code, the relationship between Nu and 0was markedly different.

![][image32]

*Fig. 18: Nusselt number vs yield stress plot for nine cases ranging from 0 1e5 \- 1e6. Where the original paper reported an abrupt jump from the stagnant cases below Nu \= 5 to the mobile or periodically mobile cases above Nu \= 10, the replicated results show a continuous series.*

![][image33]

*Fig 19: Log-log plot of the above, highlighting the apparent power law behaviour. Not only is the correlation high (*R2\>0.9) *but the error is also not significantly greater at the extremes, indicating a good fit.*

An important observation of the original paper was that the average Nu across the episodic case tracks the mobile case at steady state. This was not observed in replication. Instead, the Nusselt number appears to vary in a continuum from \~4 at 0=1e6 to \~10 at 0=1e5. Distribution is a good fit (R2\>0.9) for a power law with exponent 0.38.

This trend may seem counterintuitive, as the notion of a mode switch implies an abrupt transition. One possible interpretation is that the trend resembles effectively a mixing curve between two endmembers: the perfectly stagnant regime (Nu \~ 4\) and the perfectly mobile regime (Nu \~ 31 at this resolution, although this is likely under-resolved \- Nu approaches 40 at double resolution). In support of this hypothesis is the fact that the various episodic modes documented all share nearly identical failure profiles, with the only significant distinctions between them being the duration of the flat latent intervals and the height of the Nusselt number peaks (ranging from 28.66 to 37.07 for the slowest and fastest regimes respectively).

![][image34]

*Fig. 20: Nusselt number profiles for a typical failure cases from each of the five episodic cases in the range 0 1e5 \- 1e6. Peaks were taken between Nu local minima and set to t \= 0 at the maximum. The match is extremely close, particularly on the post-failure side.*

For the mixing hypothesis to be true, failure events from across parameter space must have the same average Nusselt number. At first glance this may not seem possible, as the Nu maxima vary by over 30% between cases. However, the peaks are so narrow that the outlier has little effect. If the Nusselt number over each peak is integrated across the time interval where Nu exceeds 7.455 \- the point of maximum curvature pre-failure for the most rapid episodic case \- and then averaged between cases, a fair estimate of the average Nu of a typical failure event is given out at 12.9. This estimation also yields an average duration of 0.0055 in dimensionless time: a good order-of-magnitude estimate for the length of an overturn cycle.

A simple formula relates the maximum a, minimum b, mean c, and relative frequency n for a system of this nature:a \- cc \- b=n. The frequency n is in this case the ratio of time spent in the stagnant mode versus time spent in the mobile mode (during a failure event). If the stagnant mode is given a flat Nu value of 4.189, and the mobile mode a value of 12.9 as derived above, a table of frequencies can be compiled for the episodic suite:

| tau0 | AvNu (t\>0.2) | Observation | n |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| 1.0E+05 | 10.374 | Mobile | *0.409* |
| 1.5E+05 | 7.3069 | Rapid episodic | 1.793 |
| 2.0E+05 | 7.0987 | Rapid episodic | 1.993 |
| 3.0E+05 | 6.5716 | Regular episodic | 2.656 |
| 4.0E+05 | 5.3760 | Paired episodic | 6.338 |
| 4.5E+05 | 5.7892 | Regular episodic | 4.443 |
| 5.0E+05 | 4.7968 | Stagnant | *13.33* |
| 6.0E+05 | 4.4272 | Stagnant | *35.56* |
| 1.0E+06 | 4.1896 | Stagnant | *1,439* |

*Fig. 21: Table of various cases of the viscoplastic model. Average Nu has been evaluated only for times greater than 0.2 to minimise the impact of initial conditions (typically causing less than a 5% discrepancy). ‘n’ is a measure of the ratio of the amount of time spent in the stagnant mode as opposed to the mobile mode; italicised values indicate cases which are in practice fully in one mode or the other.*

The ‘n’ parameter highlights some interesting features of the model suite. The lowest yield-stress stagnant case, for example, has a value of ‘n’ that would imply a latent period between failure events of \~ 0.7 if the case was episodic. But the nearest episodic case includes latent periods 10-20% longer than this. This suggests that timing is not a factor in determining the episodic to stagnant phase boundary, and that very long-wavelength failure cycles may be possible. At the other end of the scale, the mobile case has an ‘n’ value of less than a half. In other words, to achieve the mobile regime’s average Nusselt number of 10.37, an equivalent episodic case would have to spend twice as much time in a state of overturn than it does under a stagnant lid. If the average failure event duration of 0.0055 represents a single overturn cycle, and if it is supposed that it takes at least one overturn cycle to restore the stagnant lid to its proper geometry between failures, it is entirely fitting that the mobile regime should begin when ‘n’ drops below unity. A review of the nearest episodic case accentuates the point: it has an ‘n’ value perilously close to one, and only just manages to touch the stagnant endmember Nusselt minimum between each cycle.

If n \= 1 is taken to represent the transition \- which would correspond to an average Nu of 8.544 \- and the power law relation with exponent 0.38 holds, it could be estimated that the mobile to episodic transition should take place at a 0=1.42e5. Within the limitations of the numerical method, then, a yield stress of 1.5e5 is almost as close as can be gotten.

![][image35]

*Fig. 22: The episodic case where 0=1.5e5, just above the transition to the mobile regime. The frequency of failures is now so rapid that the Nu curve barely reaches the stagnant endmember values between each cycle. (More languid episodic cases not only meet, but dip below the Nusselt numbers of the most stable stagnant case.) Since the profile of each failure event is independent of yield stress, but failure frequency is strongly controlled by it, it is inevitable that decreasing 0 much below this threshold will lead to a collapse into the mobile regime as the stagnant lid is left with no time to recover in each cycle. Also shown is the average temperature profile for this case, which oscillates around a dimensionless T of 0.73.* 

### 5.2 \- Project Plan

The proposed goal of this PhD is to identify structural and geochemical lines of evidence that could constrain the timing and style of a tectonic mode transition in the early Earth. This will be achieved primarily through numerical modelling via the *Underworld2* code package, and will involve the development of a specialised wrapper optimised for planetary scale suite modelling.

In the two to three months after confirmation, the first task will be to complete development of the suite modelling code and use it to complement and complete the data presented in this report, ideally populating parameter space with sufficient density to properly constrain and characterise episodic-to-mobile and episodic-to-stagnant regimes. Depending on progress made, an effort may be made to extend this research to a logical milestone suitable for presentation in poster form at this year’s AGU Fall meeting in December (submissions close at the end of July). Promising avenues of development include reproducing these results in an annulus geometry, performing a narrow-scope, high-resolution 3D model of the stress field around a lithospheric heterogeneity, and implementing the self-organised cratonisation mechanism explored by [(Beall, Moresi, and Cooper 2018\)](https://paperpile.com/c/a2pYSk/eag7). 

If a role for continents in conditioning mantle convection can be substantiated, a good initiative for the last quarter of 2018 through to the first quarter of 2019 would be an expanded survey of this role, in which a large array of different initial continental configurations will be modelled and assessed for their impacts on the global circulation. This will also provide the impetus to develop an additional capability for the suite modelling code: automated analysis of flow geometry, determining for example whether convection is degree-one or degree-two, how many cells are present, whether they are homogeneous or heterogeneous, square or narrow, et cetera. With such a tool, large computational resources can be lavished on the task without taxing the operator for any but the most significant or ambiguous cases. It is to be hoped that such a large-scale survey will reveal attractors in continental geometry that may vindicate the model with respect to Earth history. Conversely, it may be proven that the role of continents is in fact a limited one, which is itself a significant result. In either case, a publishable paper suitable for presentation at either EGU 2019 or the Lunar and Planetary Science Conference in Houston will be the sought-after outcome of this research unit.

Ultimately, it will be necessary to ground the inquiry with natural data. One promising option involves Earth’s Archaean terranes. As the oldest cratons, they likely bear untapped structural and geochemical information relevant to the question of early Earth tectonics. [(Beall, Moresi, and Cooper 2018\)](https://paperpile.com/c/a2pYSk/eag7) have already demonstrated how extreme stress related to the collapse of a stagnant lid could explain some of the large-scale features of greenstone belts. This work should be expanded to explore the structures generated by rafting of oceanic plateaux and island arcs to the earliest cratons, a likely major contributor to the growth of the continents [(Albare\`de 1998\)](https://paperpile.com/c/a2pYSk/IwQK). A simple tectonic erosion function could also be implemented. A Monte Carlo array of such models may reveal statistically significant trends in crustal production, preservation, and destruction: competing trends that have proved difficult to unpick from geochemical data alone [(Hawkesworth, Cawood, and Dhuime 2013\)](https://paperpile.com/c/a2pYSk/ZXMA). More exciting still is the possibility that a sufficiently comprehensive model of continent/mantle interactions may be able to sustain a self-organised supercontinent cycle. This research unit should be expected to fully occupy the last year of the PhD program from mid-2019 to mid-2020 and will ideally support a second publishable paper.

## 6 \- Conclusion

The question of the origins of plate tectonics is pertinent to some of humanity’s largest preoccupations. Central to resolving this conundrum is the study of tectonic mode transitions, and the various feedbacks that preference one mode of global circulation over another. In this report, a hypothesis regarding a crucial role for ancient buoyant crust in Earth’s stagnant-to-mobile transition has been set out, along with a feasible program for tackling the problem in the timeframe of a PhD. Progress has included development of a new set of code tools tailored for the large-scale suite modelling efforts this program demands. These tools have been benchmarked on [(Louis Moresi and Solomatov 1998\)](https://paperpile.com/c/a2pYSk/pBL7), with whose results this replication study significantly agrees. Certain divergent results, including a possible power-law relationship between Nusselt number and yield stress and the existence of a long-wavelength pseudostagnant regime are exciting and worthwhile short-term science objectives. More importantly, the results presented here provide a robust stepping-off point for an inquiry into the role of continents in tectonic mode transitions, with implications for Australia’s own Archaean terranes as well as farther-afield topics such as the divergent tectonic modes of Earth, Mars, and Venus.
